title: Quadratic Equations: Roots and Forming Equations
summary: What a quadratic equation is, what its roots are, how the sum and product of the roots are linked to the coefficients, and how to build an equation from its roots.

p: A quadratic equation is an equation in which the highest power of the unknown is 2. Its standard form is ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b and c are numbers and a is not 0. For example, x² − 5x + 6 = 0 has a = 1, b = −5 and c = 6.
The values of x that make the equation true are called the roots (or solutions) of the equation. A quadratic equation has at most two roots.

To test whether a number is a root, put it in place of x. If the left side becomes 0, it is a root. Test x = 2 in x² − 5x + 6: 4 − 10 + 6 = 0. So x = 2 is a root. Test x = 4: 16 − 20 + 6 = 2, which is not 0, so x = 4 is not a root.

sections.h: Sum and product of the roots
p: Suppose the roots of a quadratic equation are α and β (alpha and beta). Then the equation can be written (x − α)(x − β) = 0. Expand it: x² − (α + β)x + αβ = 0.
So, for x² + (b/a)x + c/a = 0, that is for ax² + bx + c = 0 with both sides divided by a:
Sum of the roots = α + β = −b/a. Product of the roots = αβ = c/a.
Example: for 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, the sum of the roots is 7/2 and the product is 3/2. You can check: the roots are 3 and 1/2. Their sum is 3½ = 7/2 and their product is 3/2. Correct.

sections.h: Forming an equation from its roots
p: Use this rule: x² − (sum of roots)x + (product of roots) = 0.
Example 1. Roots 2 and 3. Sum = 5, product = 6. The equation is x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
Example 2. Roots −1 and 4. Sum = 3, product = −4. The equation is x² − 3x − 4 = 0.

Example 3. Roots 1/2 and −3. Sum = 1/2 − 3 = −5/2 and product = −3/2. The equation is x² + (5/2)x − 3/2 = 0. Multiply every term by 2 to remove the fractions: 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0. Check x = 1/2: 2 × 1/4 + 5/2 − 3 = 0.5 + 2.5 − 3 = 0. Correct.
One root of x² − 5x + k = 0 is 2. Find k. Put x = 2: 4 − 10 + k = 0, so k = 6. The equation is x² − 5x + 6 = 0 and the other root is 3 (because the sum of the roots is 5).

activity: Without solving, write down the sum and the product of the roots of 3x² − 6x − 2 = 0 (sum 2, product −2/3). Then form the quadratic equation whose roots are −2 and 5 (x² − 3x − 10 = 0).

title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Factorisation
summary: Writing a quadratic equation in the form ax² + bx + c = 0 and factorising it, then using the rule that if two things multiply to give 0, one of them is 0.

p: If A × B = 0, then A = 0 or B = 0 (or both). This is called the zero product rule. So if we can write a quadratic as a product of two brackets equal to 0, each bracket gives one root.
Important: first move every term to one side so that the other side is 0. For example x² = 5x − 6 must first be written x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
Find two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b.
Example: x² − 5x + 6 = 0. Two numbers with product 6 and sum −5 are −2 and −3. So (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. Therefore x = 2 or x = 3.
Example: x² + x − 12 = 0. Two numbers with product −12 and sum +1 are +4 and −3. So (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0. Therefore x = −4 or x = 3.

sections.h: Case 2: when a is not 1 (splitting the middle term)
p: Multiply a by c. Find two numbers with that product and with sum b. Use them to split the middle term, then factorise in pairs.
Example: 2x² + 7x + 3 = 0. a × c = 6. Two numbers with product 6 and sum 7 are 6 and 1. So 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 0. Group: 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = 0, so (2x + 1)(x + 3) = 0. Therefore x = −1/2 or x = −3.

Example: 6x² − x − 2 = 0. a × c = −12. Two numbers with product −12 and sum −1 are −4 and +3. So 6x² − 4x + 3x − 2 = 0. Group: 2x(3x − 2) + 1(3x − 2) = 0, so (3x − 2)(2x + 1) = 0. Therefore x = 2/3 or x = −1/2.
Difference of two squares: x² − 9 = 0 gives (x − 3)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 3 or x = −3.
No constant term: x² − 3x = 0 gives x(x − 3) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 3. Never divide both sides by x, because you will lose the root x = 0.
Put each root back in the original equation. For x = −4 in x² + x − 12: 16 − 4 − 12 = 0. Correct.

title: Solving Quadratic Equations by Completing the Square
summary: A method that works for every quadratic equation, even when the roots are not whole numbers: make one side a perfect square.

p: A perfect square looks like (x + p)² = x² + 2px + p². Notice that the number at the end, p², is the square of half the coefficient of x. So to turn x² + bx into a perfect square, add (b/2)².
Examples: x² + 10x needs 25 to become (x + 5)². x² − 6x needs 9 to become (x − 3)². x² + x needs 1/4 to become (x + 1/2)².
1. Make the coefficient of x² equal to 1 (divide every term by a if a is not 1).
2. Move the constant term to the right side.
3. Add (half the coefficient of x)² to both sides.
4. Write the left side as a square, then take the square root of both sides. Remember ±.
5. Solve for x.

title: Solving Quadratic Equations by the Formula
summary: The quadratic formula x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, with worked examples where the roots are whole numbers, fractions and surds.

p: If we complete the square on ax² + bx + c = 0 in the same way as in the last unit, the result is always the same:
This is the quadratic formula. It works for every quadratic equation, so it is the safest method when factorising is hard.
1. Write the equation as ax² + bx + c = 0 and list a, b, c with their signs.
2. Work out b² − 4ac first (this is called the discriminant).
3. Substitute into the formula, then work out the + answer and the − answer.

title: Nature of Roots: The Discriminant
summary: Using b² − 4ac to tell, without solving, whether a quadratic equation has two different real roots, two equal roots or no real roots.

p: In the quadratic formula the part under the square root, D = b² − 4ac, decides what kind of roots we get. It is called the discriminant because it discriminates (tells apart) the different cases.
See the table below. Remember that you cannot take the square root of a negative number in real numbers.

head: Value of D
Roots
Graph touches the x-axis
rows: Two equal real roots (one repeated root)

p: D = 16 − 16 = 0. So the roots are equal. Indeed (x − 2)² = 0, so x = 2 twice.
D = 4 − 20 = −16. D is negative, so there are no real roots.
D = 9 + 16 = 25. D is positive, so there are two different real roots. Also, 25 is a perfect square, so the roots are rational: x = (3 ± 5)/4, so x = 2 or x = −1/2.
Find k so that x² + kx + 9 = 0 has equal roots. For equal roots, D = 0: k² − 4(1)(9) = 0, so k² = 36 and k = 6 or k = −6.
For which values of k does x² + 4x + k = 0 have real roots? We need D ≥ 0: 16 − 4k ≥ 0, so k ≤ 4.

title: Word Problems with Quadratic Equations
summary: Turning everyday and number problems into quadratic equations, solving them and rejecting answers that do not make sense.

p: 1. Read the problem and choose a letter for the unknown. Write down what it stands for.
2. Write the other quantities using that letter.
3. Form an equation from the facts given.
4. Rearrange to ax² + bx + c = 0 and solve.
5. Check each answer in the problem. Reject any answer that is impossible (for example a negative length).

The product of two consecutive positive integers is 56. Find them. Let the integers be n and n + 1. n(n + 1) = 56, so n² + n − 56 = 0. (n + 8)(n − 7) = 0. n = 7 or n = −8. They are positive, so n = 7 and the numbers are 7 and 8. (If negative numbers were allowed, −8 and −7 would also work.)

The length of a rectangle is 3 cm more than its width. Its area is 40 cm². Find its dimensions. Let the width be w. Then length = w + 3. w(w + 3) = 40, so w² + 3w − 40 = 0. (w + 8)(w − 5) = 0. w = 5 or w = −8. A width cannot be negative, so w = 5 cm and length = 8 cm. Check: 5 × 8 = 40. Correct.

The two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle are x cm and (x + 7) cm. The hypotenuse is 13 cm. Find x. By Pythagoras, x² + (x + 7)² = 13². x² + x² + 14x + 49 = 169. 2x² + 14x − 120 = 0. Divide by 2: x² + 7x − 60 = 0. (x + 12)(x − 5) = 0. x = 5 (reject −12). The sides are 5 cm, 12 cm and 13 cm. Check: 25 + 144 = 169. Correct.

sections.h: Problem 4: a number and its square
p: A number added to its square gives 30. x² + x − 30 = 0. (x + 6)(x − 5) = 0. The number is 5 or −6. Both work: 25 + 5 = 30 and 36 − 6 = 30.

title: Simultaneous Linear Equations
summary: Solving two linear equations in two unknowns by elimination and by substitution, and checking the answer.

p: Two equations with two unknowns, such as x + y = 10 and x − y = 2, have a pair of values of x and y that work in both equations at the same time. To find them we remove (eliminate) one unknown, or we replace one unknown with an expression (substitute).

Example 1: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2. The y terms are +y and −y, so add the equations: 3x = 9, so x = 3. Put x = 3 in x − y = 2: 3 − y = 2, so y = 1. Check in 2x + y: 6 + 1 = 7. Correct. Answer: x = 3, y = 1.
Example 2: 3x + 2y = 16 and x + y = 6. Multiply the second equation by 2: 2x + 2y = 12. Subtract this from the first: x = 4. Then y = 6 − 4 = 2. Check: 12 + 4 = 16. Correct.

Example 3 (multiply both): 2x + 3y = 13 and 3x − 2y = 0. Multiply the first by 2: 4x + 6y = 26. Multiply the second by 3: 9x − 6y = 0. Add: 13x = 26, so x = 2. Put in the first: 4 + 3y = 13, so y = 3. Check the second: 6 − 6 = 0. Correct.

sections.h: Rule for choosing add or subtract
p: Make the numbers in front of one letter the same size. If their signs are the same, subtract the equations. If their signs are different, add the equations.
Example: y = 2x − 1 and 3x + y = 9. Replace y in the second equation: 3x + 2x − 1 = 9, so 5x = 10 and x = 2. Then y = 2(2) − 1 = 3. Check: 6 + 3 = 9. Correct. Answer: x = 2, y = 3.

title: One Linear and One Quadratic Equation
summary: Solving simultaneous equations when one is linear and the other is quadratic, by substitution. There are usually two pairs of answers.

p: 1. Make one letter the subject of the linear equation.
2. Substitute it into the quadratic equation. You get a quadratic equation in one letter.
3. Solve it. You usually get two values.
4. Put each value into the linear equation to find the matching value of the other letter. Always use the linear equation for this, because it is easier and avoids false pairs.

sections.h: Example 1: a line and a circle
p: y = x + 1 and x² + y² = 25. Substitute: x² + (x + 1)² = 25. 2x² + 2x + 1 = 25, so 2x² + 2x − 24 = 0, so x² + x − 12 = 0. (x + 4)(x − 3) = 0. x = 3 gives y = 4. x = −4 gives y = −3. Solutions: (3, 4) and (−4, −3). Check (−4, −3): 16 + 9 = 25. Correct.

sections.h: Example 2: a line and a parabola
p: y = 2x − 3 and y = x² − 2x − 3. The two y values are equal, so x² − 2x − 3 = 2x − 3. x² − 4x = 0, so x(x − 4) = 0. x = 0 gives y = −3. x = 4 gives y = 5. Solutions: (0, −3) and (4, 5). You will see these on a graph in Unit 24.

x + y = 5 and xy = 6. From the first, y = 5 − x. So x(5 − x) = 6, which gives 5x − x² = 6, so x² − 5x + 6 = 0. (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. x = 2 gives y = 3 and x = 3 gives y = 2. Solutions: (2, 3) and (3, 2).

sections.h: Example 4: x − y = 1 and x² + y² = 13
p: x = y + 1. Substitute: (y + 1)² + y² = 13. 2y² + 2y + 1 = 13, so y² + y − 6 = 0. (y + 3)(y − 2) = 0. y = 2 gives x = 3. y = −3 gives x = −2. Solutions: (3, 2) and (−2, −3). Check: 4 + 9 = 13. Correct.

title: Word Problems with Simultaneous Equations
summary: Forming two equations from a story, solving them, and checking that the answers fit the story.

p: Choose two letters for the two unknowns. Write two equations, one from each fact in the story. Solve and check against both facts.

Three pens and two books cost ₦1 100. Two pens and three books cost ₦1 150. Find the price of each. Let a pen cost p naira and a book cost b naira. 3p + 2b = 1 100 and 2p + 3b = 1 150. Multiply the first by 3: 9p + 6b = 3 300. Multiply the second by 2: 4p + 6b = 2 300. Subtract: 5p = 1 000, so p = 200. Then 2b = 1 100 − 600 = 500, so b = 250. Check: 400 + 750 = 1 150. Correct. A pen costs ₦200 and a book costs ₦250.
Two numbers add up to 12 and their product is 35. Find them. x + y = 12 and xy = 35. y = 12 − x, so x(12 − x) = 35, which gives x² − 12x + 35 = 0. (x − 5)(x − 7) = 0. The numbers are 5 and 7.

The perimeter of a rectangle is 28 cm and its area is 48 cm². Find the sides. Half the perimeter is 14, so l + w = 14 and lw = 48. l = 14 − w, so w(14 − w) = 48, giving w² − 14w + 48 = 0. (w − 6)(w − 8) = 0. The sides are 6 cm and 8 cm.

Adult tickets cost ₦300 and child tickets cost ₦100. 20 tickets were sold for ₦4 000. Let a = adults and c = children. a + c = 20 and 300a + 100c = 4 000, which simplifies to 3a + c = 40. Subtract the first equation: 2a = 20, so a = 10 and c = 10. Check: 3 000 + 1 000 = 4 000. Correct.

title: Graphs of Linear Equations
summary: Drawing a straight line from a table of values, finding the gradient and intercepts, and writing an equation from two points.

sections.h: The equation of a straight line
p: Any equation that can be written y = mx + c has a straight-line graph. m is the gradient (the steepness) and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis).
Gradient = rise / run = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁).

sections.h: Drawing a line from a table
p: Draw y = 2x + 1. Choose some values of x and work out y.

img.alt: Graph of the straight line y = 2x + 1 showing the y-intercept at (0, 1), the x-intercept at (-0.5, 0) and a run of 1 and rise of 2
img.cap: The line y = 2x + 1. For every 1 step right it goes 2 steps up.

p: The line crosses the y-axis at (0, 1), so c = 1. It crosses the x-axis where y = 0: 2x + 1 = 0, so x = −1/2. The gradient is 2: for each 1 unit across, the line rises 2 units.
Tips for graphs: draw straight lines with a ruler and a sharp pencil, use a suitable scale, label both axes, and write the equation next to the line.

sections.h: Finding the gradient and equation from two points
p: The line passes through (1, 3) and (3, 7). Gradient m = (7 − 3)/(3 − 1) = 4/2 = 2. So y = 2x + c. Put in (1, 3): 3 = 2 + c, so c = 1. The equation is y = 2x + 1.

sections.h: Intercepts of a line in another form
p: For 2x + 3y = 6: when x = 0, y = 2, so the y-intercept is (0, 2). When y = 0, x = 3, so the x-intercept is (3, 0). Rearranged: 3y = −2x + 6, so y = −(2/3)x + 2. The gradient is −2/3 (the line slopes downward).
Lines with the same gradient are parallel. y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 5 never meet.

title: Graphs of Quadratic Equations
summary: Drawing the curve (parabola) y = ax² + bx + c from a table, and reading its roots, turning point, axis of symmetry and intercepts.

sections.h: The shape of a quadratic graph
p: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a smooth curve called a parabola. If a is positive the curve is U-shaped and has a lowest point (a minimum). If a is negative it is shaped like an upside-down U and has a highest point (a maximum). This point is called the turning point or vertex.
The curve is symmetrical about a vertical line through the turning point, called the axis of symmetry. Its equation is x = −b/(2a).
Make a table of values and work out y for each x. For x = −2: 4 + 4 − 3 = 5. For x = 3: 9 − 6 − 3 = 0.

img.alt: Graph of the parabola y = x squared minus 2x minus 3 with roots at -1 and 3, minimum point (1, -4), y-intercept (0, -3) and axis of symmetry x = 1

p: Roots: where the curve crosses the x-axis, x = −1 and x = 3. These are the solutions of x² − 2x − 3 = 0. Check by factorising: (x + 1)(x − 3) = 0.
y-intercept: (0, −3). The number c is always the y-intercept.
Turning point: the lowest point is (1, −4). The axis of symmetry is x = 1, which is halfway between the roots: (−1 + 3)/2 = 1.
Notice that the table is symmetrical: the y values 5, 0, −3 on the left come back as −3, 0, 5 on the right.

sections.h: A graph with a maximum: y = 3 + 2x − x²
p: Here a = −1 (negative), so the curve is an upside-down U. Table: x = −1 gives 3 − 2 − 1 = 0. x = 0 gives 3. x = 1 gives 3 + 2 − 1 = 4. x = 2 gives 3 + 4 − 4 = 3. x = 3 gives 3 + 6 − 9 = 0. The maximum point is (1, 4) and the roots are −1 and 3.
Use at least seven points. Plot them carefully with small crosses. Join them with a smooth curve drawn freehand, not with a ruler. The bottom of the curve should be round, not pointed.

title: Solving Equations Graphically
summary: Using a drawn parabola to solve quadratic equations, and using a straight line drawn on the same axes to solve other equations and simultaneous equations.

p: The solution of an equation is where two graphs meet. If one graph is the curve and the other is a line, the x-coordinates of the crossing points are the solutions.
Take y = x² − 2x − 3 (drawn in the last unit). The equation says y = 0, so the roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis: x = −1 and x = 3.

Draw the line y = 2 on the same axes. It crosses the curve at two points. Read the x-values: x ≈ −1.45 and x ≈ 3.45. Check by algebra: x² − 2x − 5 = 0 gives x = 1 ± √6 = 1 ± 2.449, so x = −1.45 or x = 3.45. The graph answer agrees.

sections.h: Solving a different equation with the same curve
p: Solve x² − 3x − 4 = 0 using the graph of y = x² − 2x − 3. Rearrange so that x² − 2x − 3 appears: x² − 3x − 4 = (x² − 2x − 3) − (x + 1). So the equation becomes x² − 2x − 3 = x + 1. Draw the line y = x + 1 and read the crossing points: x = −1 and x = 4. Check: at x = 4 the line gives y = 5 and the curve gives 16 − 8 − 3 = 5. They meet.
Solve y = x² − 2x − 3 and y = 2x − 3 together. Draw both on the same axes. They cross at (0, −3) and (4, 5), which matches the algebra from Unit 20.

4. Solve x + y = 7 and x − y = 1: add: 2x = 8, x = 4, y = 3.
5. Nature of the roots of 3x² + 2x + 1 = 0: D = 4 − 12 = −8. No real roots.
6. Form the equation whose roots are 4 and −1: sum = 3, product = −4, so x² − 3x − 4 = 0.

Show every step of your working. Check answers by substituting. Read each problem twice. Write units. Draw graphs with a ruler and sharp pencil, label the axes and give the graph a title. Practise a little every day instead of cramming.
